Draft-aligned decoding of a 30B diffusion model

A small model writes the block. A 39-million-parameter adapter teaches the big model to judge it. This is what the mechanism is, why it should work, and what actually happened.

SDAR-30B-A3B · block 32 branch drafter-voting 6-7 September 2026

Read this before the numbers

The trained judge ties the training-free baseline; it does not beat it. The best trained setting reaches 94.0% accuracy at 7.93 passes per block. A rule that needs no training at all reaches 95.0% at the same 7.93 passes. Round 1 of training failed outright at 38.0%. Round 2a is a large qualitative repair of round 1, and a real mechanism result, but it is not yet a better speed/accuracy frontier.

All decode comparisons below are on 100 prompts, so a 95% interval is about ±5 accuracy points. Only the training-free rule has been confirmed on a 500-item held-out set.

01

The machine you are trying to speed up

Everything downstream follows from three facts about how this particular model writes text. None of them hold for an ordinary autoregressive LLM.

It writes 32 tokens at a time, not one. SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32 is a block-diffusion language model. It takes a block of 32 empty slots, each holding a special [MASK] token, and runs one forward pass over the whole sequence. That pass produces a probability distribution over the full 151,936-token vocabulary at every one of the 32 slots simultaneously, each conditioned on the prompt, on all previously finished blocks, and on whatever is currently sitting in the other 31 slots.

It commits only where it is already sure. After the pass, a slot is filled in permanently if its top token's probability exceeds 0.95. Everything else stays [MASK] and is looked at again next pass. At least one slot is forced to commit per pass so the loop cannot stall. Repeat until the block is full, then run one more forward pass to write the finished block into the key/value cache. I will call each of these forwards a pass.

Each pass is expensive in a specific way. The model is a mixture of experts: 48 layers, and in each layer 128 separate feed-forward "experts", of which each token position picks its own top 8. With 32 positions × 8 picks per layer, the union of experts that must actually be loaded from memory is far larger than 8 — measured at 43.1 experts per layer when the block is all masks, and 64.5 when it is full of tokens. Since the weights of an expert must be fetched to run it, the honest cost unit is the expert-layer execution: one expert, running at one layer, in one pass. Divided by the tokens the model actually produced, this is the number to reduce.

02

Why it takes nine passes when one would do

The block does not need nine passes because the model is unsure what to say. It needs nine passes because of the difference between a marginal and a conditional distribution.

Consider one slot in the middle of an otherwise empty block. The model is being asked: what token goes here, given the prompt and given that everything around it is still unknown? The text could continue "So the total is", or "Therefore the total is", or "The total is therefore". All three are correct. The model's probability splits across them — 0.4 / 0.35 / 0.25, say. Nothing reaches 0.95, so nothing commits, even though any of the three would have been fine.

Formally, the distribution at an open slot is a marginal over every completion of the block that is consistent with what has been committed:

p(xi | committed) = Σrest p(xi, rest | committed) ← flat wherever phrasing is free p(xi | committed, rest = D) ← peaked: one concrete completion to judge

A slot whose token is forced by the prefix — the second digit of "10 × 2 = 20" — gets 0.99 and commits immediately. So pass 1 commits only the forced slots, on average 7.5 of the 29.4 generated slots in a block. Each commit then forces a few more slots, which commit next pass, which force a few more. That chain is the nine passes.

The waste is measurable and large. At pass 1 the model's own top guess already equals the token the block eventually ends with at 58.4% of slots — but only 25.6% of slots pass the threshold. A third of all tokens in the finished text are right at pass 1 and committed later anyway, purely because the marginal was too flat to clear 0.95.

The second line of the equation is the whole idea. If some other process proposes one concrete completion D for the rest of the block, then every slot becomes a conditional question — "is this token right, given these specific neighbours?" — and conditional questions are peaked where marginal ones are flat. Judging is easy where generating is hard.

03

The proposal: a 1.7B model writes the block first

A small dense model of the same family, SDAR-1.7B-Chat-b32, fills all 32 slots in 8 of its own cheap denoising steps. Its guess D becomes the concrete completion the big model conditions on.

How good is the draft, and what does it cost

drafter settingslot agreement with the big model forwards / blockms / forward
4 static steps0.4973.9818.1
8 static steps (used)0.5587.8618.0
dynamic, threshold .900.58610.5918.0
the 30B itself, one pass on an empty block— 1.00369

Agreement 0.558 means: for a randomly chosen slot, the 1.7B's token is the token the 30B eventually writes there, 55.8% of the time. That number is the hard ceiling on how much any draft-based scheme can save, and it is also why this is not classical speculative decoding — more on that below.

The cost arithmetic is favourable and simple. Eight drafter forwards cost 8 × 18 = 144 ms, against 369 ms for a single forward of the big model on an empty block. So the entire draft costs about 0.4 of one big-model pass. The draft is worth it if it removes more than about half a pass out of 9.31. The target was to remove five or six.

Why this is not speculative decoding

In classical speculative decoding the big model is autoregressive, so its output at position i is by construction a judgement of the token at i+1, produced without having seen it. The verifier is free, exact, and acceptance is a prefix: reject the third drafted token and the fourth is discarded too, because it assumed the third. At 56% agreement the accepted prefix averages about two tokens — which is what earlier work on this branch found.

Here the big model has bidirectional attention inside the block. There is no free verifier, but acceptance is per slot: the judge reads all 32 at once, so its verdict on slot 20 can be right when slot 17 was wrong. At 56% agreement that is ~18 slots per pass instead of ~2. That is the prize, and it is exactly what a causal verifier cannot deliver.

04

The obstacle: the stock model cannot read a filled slot

This is the finding the whole project turns on, and it is a property of how SDAR was trained, not a bug in our code.

SDAR's training loss is computed only at [MASK] positions. That is the standard masked-diffusion objective: corrupt some tokens to the absorbing [MASK] state, predict them back, score nothing else. It means that at a slot which already holds a token, the model's output logits were never supervised by a single gradient step in 50 billion tokens of continued training.

So what does come out of a filled slot? The base model underneath SDAR is Qwen3, an ordinary autoregressive next-token predictor, and that behaviour survives untouched at exactly the positions diffusion training never visited. We measured it directly by filling a block with the model's own final tokens and reading every slot:

block filled with the FINAL tokens, read at slot i: argmax = token at slot i+1 ... 93.6% (of slots that have a successor) argmax = token at slot i ... 10.0% block filled with the DRAFT tokens, read at slot i: argmax = draft token at i+1 ... 84.8%

Reading a filled slot on the stock model gives you a shifted copy of the input. It is not a judgement of anything. This single fact explains every earlier failed attempt on this branch to "show the model the draft and ask it what it thinks".

Three ways to ask, and what each one actually returns

Since we cannot read a filled slot, there are only three remaining ways to get an opinion about a draft token out of the frozen model. We probed all three on 87 items, 537 blocks, 15,782 slots.

The halves trick fails for an interesting reason. Keeping the judged slot masked puts it back in the trained regime, and confidence duly explodes: the share of slots clearing 0.95 rises from 0.26 to 0.90. But the model agrees with the draft at 92% of slots, and specifically confirms 76% of the drafter's wrong tokens at above 0.95, while correcting a wrong draft in only 1.2% of slots. It is not verifying; it is deferring.

The control that proves this is deference and not competence: fill the context with the model's own incoherent pass-1 guesses instead of the drafter's coherent block, and the confirmation rate collapses from 33.4% of slots to 6.6%. The stock model is a sycophantic verifier of any coherent context. It trusts fluency, not correctness. Decoding end to end this way gives 67.0% accuracy against a 95.0% baseline. Closed.

The conclusion that motivates training

The ability "judge whether this specific token belongs in this specific slot, given its neighbours" does not exist anywhere in the frozen model. No threshold, no voting scheme, no clever masking pattern can extract it, because there is nothing to extract. If we want that ability, we have to put it there.

05

The training-free baseline, and why it is hard to beat

The third readout — the model's own opinion of the draft, formed before it saw the draft — costs nothing and works. It is the baseline everything else must beat.

The big model's very first pass on a block is run anyway, with the block empty. From those same logits, read qi = the probability the model assigns to the drafter's token at slot i. This number is uncontaminated: the model never saw the draft. If it is above a threshold γ, take the drafter's token for that slot even though the model's own top-1 did not clear 0.95. Zero extra forward passes. I will call this the free rule.

accept Di ⇔ slot i still open ∧ pMoE(Di | empty block) > γ

At γ = 0.50 the rule takes about 4.7 extra slots per block and gets 0.43 of them wrong. That turns out to be free in practice, because a wrong token in a slot the block later contradicts is usually re-derived: end to end, accuracy is exactly unchanged, item for item, while passes fall 15%.

A paired 95% interval on the held-out 500 items is +0.2 [−1.4, +1.8] points — accuracy-neutral, with 16% fewer passes and 13% less expert work. Modest, but real, confirmed on data never used for tuning, and free. It is also the decoder that generated all the training data.

06

Building the missing verifier

The plan is to teach the model, and only the model, one new behaviour: at a slot that holds a tentative draft token, output the token that actually belongs there rather than a copy of the next input.

What is trained

Nothing large. The experts, the embeddings, the output head and the drafter are all frozen. The trainable set is a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the four attention projections of all 48 layers, plus one vector:

trainable partwhereparameters
LoRA rank 32, α = 64, on q, k, v, oall 48 layers26,738,688
the draft-flag vectoradded to input embeddings2,048
total, round 2a26,740,736  (0.09% of 30.5 B)
round 1 also trained the 128-way router gatesall 48 layers +12,582,912

LoRA writes W x + (α/r)·B A x with thin trainable A and B, and B initialised to zero, so training starts at exactly the stock model. Attention is the right place for this update: "copy the token at my own slot" is an identity attention pattern and "infer a slot from its neighbours" is the masked-slot machinery SDAR already has. The adapter's job is to change which of the two fires at a filled slot — a change in where attention looks, which is precisely what a low-rank update to q, k, v, o can express.

What one training example is

One example is an (item, block) pair, and its state is re-randomised every time it is drawn. This corruption process is the heart of the method, because it must reproduce the states the judge will actually meet:

  • with probability 0.4, nothing is committed — the pass-1 state;
  • otherwise, a recorded denoising pass is drawn and its committed set is used;
  • each still-open slot then holds the drafter's token with probability 1−m and [MASK] with probability m, with m uniform on [0,1];
  • with probability 0.3, m = 0 exactly — every open slot draft-filled, the literal pass-1 inference state.

Crucially, the corruption is the real drafter's own errors, not uniform noise. Prior work on correcting filled tokens in diffusion models corrupts with random or self-sampled tokens; here the wrong tokens the judge must learn to catch are exactly the wrong tokens it will meet.

CCD C▨D D▨C DD▨

C committed — input only, no loss D draft token — input only, never a target ▨ [MASK]

The targets, and the loss

The target at every open slot is the token that block ended up with in the big model's own decode — specifically, the free rule's decode from section 5, keeping only items whose final answer was correct. Quality is protected by the targets being the model's own outputs, not by any exactness argument. Where the draft was right, the target equals it (a confirmation); where it was wrong, the target differs (an override).

L = meani∈O [ −log pi(Ti) ] cross-entropy, all open slots + β · meani∈C H( softmax(zi / τ) ) sharpen, only where already right O = open slots, C = { i ∈ O : argmax pi = Ti } β = 2.0, τ = 0.5, the [MASK] column removed before H

The first term teaches what to say. The second is dParallel's certainty forcing: where the model's top guess is already the target, push its probability toward 1 so the slot clears the 0.95 commit threshold in one pass instead of three. It is never applied to a wrong slot, so it sharpens a correct distribution rather than entrenching a wrong one. The [MASK] column is removed because entropy could otherwise be minimised by piling probability on a token that is never a legal output.

Not in the loss: the drafter; any pull toward the original model; committed slots; prefix tokens.

The budget, and its honest smallness

Round 1 and round 2a both trained on 3,000 GSM8K prompts → 2,843 correct → 16,905 blocks (16,334 train / 571 held out, split by item so no block of a held-out item is ever trained on). Two epochs at a global batch of 32 states is 1,057 optimiser steps, AdamW at 2e−5, cosine decay, ~5.3 s per step on 8 GPUs. With ~20 open slots per block that is roughly 600,000 supervised slots — 7 to 15 times less than dParallel used for a comparable behaviour change. Under-confidence was flagged in advance as the first thing to go wrong, and it is exactly what went wrong.

07

Round 1 failed, and the failure was informative

The first adapter had no draft flag and no gate. It was worse than doing nothing.

The diagnostic is a single comparison. At draft-filled slots, round 1's held-out accuracy reached 0.393. The trivial policy "just copy the input token" scores 0.556, because that is the drafter's agreement rate. The trained judge was well below the do-nothing baseline.

Two structural causes, both fixed in round 2a:

  1. The model could not tell a guess from a fact. In round 1's input, a tentative draft token and a permanently committed token are byte-identical. So the judge had to first infer which slots it was even being asked about — impossible when the drafter's mistakes are plausible. At inference we know exactly which slots are drafts, and we were withholding it. Every speculative-decoding verifier is told; every diffusion model is told its noise level. We told it nothing.
  2. The adapter leaked. One delta applied at every position let the judging task bleed into masked and committed slots, disturbing ordinary decoding.

Round 2a adds the flag and the gate, freezes the router gates, keeps the same data and the same 1,057-step budget, and is trained from scratch — so any gain is attributable to the mechanism and not to more compute.

The repair is unambiguous at the level of the mechanism. Held-out accuracy at draft slots goes 0.393 → 0.579, finally above the 0.556 copy baseline; confident commits go from 77% right to 96% right; and the all-mask regime stays pinned at the stock value through every evaluation, exactly as the gating guarantees.

08

How the trained judge decodes

One forward pass per round, with every open slot holding the draft, and a three-way verdict per slot.

  1. The drafter writes the block in 8 steps → D.
  2. The big model runs one forward pass with every open slot holding D — no masks at all — and the draft flag armed at exactly those slots.
  3. Per slot: commit to the judge's argmax if its probability beats τ; otherwise keep the draft as tentative context if the judge's argmax agrees with it; otherwise re-mask the slot.
  4. Repeat on the new state. At least one commit is forced per pass, so it terminates. Then the cache flush, as always.

Step 3 is the part with no analogue in speculative decoding. A rejected slot does not discard the slots after it; it just goes back to being a question, with everything the pass did settle now available as context.

09

Where the remaining errors come from

The judge's mistakes are not spread evenly. They live almost entirely in one of its two kinds of decision, and that is what makes the result diagnosable rather than merely disappointing.

Split every confident commit in two. A confirmation is a commit where the judge's argmax equals the drafter's token — it agrees. An override is a commit where the argmax differs — it overrules the draft. On 8,687 held-out pass-1 slots, at τ = 0.95:

Nearly every wrong confident commit is an override. When the judge agrees with the draft it is right 99 times in 100; when it overrules the draft it is wrong 17 times in 100. Raising only the override threshold to 0.99 lifts override precision to 0.953 and cuts expected damage from 0.46 wrong commits per block to 0.14 — which is exactly the asymmetric rule in the results table, and exactly why it recovers accuracy.

But it recovers accuracy by giving the pass savings back, and that is the crux:

Why the judge ties instead of winning

Confirmations are capped and overrides are unreliable. Confirmations can never exceed the drafter's 55.5% agreement, and the judge is confident enough to take only 62% of the correct drafts it sees. The decisions that would break through that ceiling — overrides, where the judge contributes something the drafter could not — are precisely the 17%-wrong ones. Make them safe and they nearly vanish; leave them loose and they cost accuracy.

The failure mode is visible in the generated text. Stock and the free rule never break the answer format. The judge at τ = .95 breaks it in 2 or 3 of its 9 wrong answers: correct reasoning ending in \boxed{180$. with a missing brace, or boxed{64}$ with a missing backslash. A wrong override of a single token in the answer wrapper flips the whole item. Under confirm .90 / override .99 no format failures occur at all — all six wrong answers are genuine reasoning errors.

10

What is settled, what is not, and what would change it

Settled

  • The mechanism findings. Filled slots on a masked-diffusion model return the next input token; draft context makes the stock model sycophantic; the empty-block marginal is the only honest free signal. These are clean measurements on 15,782 slots and they explain a family of failed approaches.
  • The training-free rule works and is held out. +0.2 accuracy points [−1.4, +1.8] with 16% fewer passes on GSM8K-500.
  • The flag-and-gate design is the right fix for round 1. 0.393 → 0.579 at draft slots, 38% → 94% end to end, at identical data and budget, with normal decoding provably untouched.
  • Draft-informed expert pools cover better than mask-informed ones. A top-32 pool voted from a draft-filled block covers 0.754 of the final tokens' expert picks against 0.511 from masks, paired difference +0.242 [+0.233, +0.252]. This lever has been measured but never yet put in a decode.

Not settled

  • Whether the judge can beat the free rule at all. On present evidence it ties. Every trained point sits on or inside the free-rule frontier.
  • Whether any of this survives 500 items. The trained results are 100-item numbers with ±5-point intervals. A 1-point deficit is not distinguishable from a 3-point one.
  • The pre-registered gates are not met. The target was accuracy within 1.5 points at ≤5 passes per block and ≤582 expert-layer executions per token. Best achieved: 1 point at 7.93 passes and 995 executions.
  • The T0 control never ran. Without the same recipe trained without a draft, we cannot yet separate "the draft helps" from "certainty forcing helps".

The three levers still open

  1. Confirmation recall. The judge's confident share was still climbing when the learning rate decayed (0.35 → 0.39 over the last 400 steps). More data and more steps should convert correct-but-timid confirmations into commits — the cheapest possible win, since confirmations are already 99% precise. running
  2. Override precision. Same route: the overrides are the only decisions that can push past the drafter's ceiling, and they need to get from 0.83 to about 0.95 at τ = .95 rather than at τ = .99. running
  3. The drafter's 55.5% agreement itself. Fine-tune the 1.7B on the big model's own trajectories, which is standard practice for speculative-decoding drafters and directly raises the cap on confirmations. queued

Running right now

Round-2 data generation is on all 8 GPUs: the remaining GSM8K prompts, a third of MATH train, and MBPP. The snapshot at the time of writing is about 38,600 usable blocks, roughly 2.3× round 1. When it finishes, an orchestrator trains the drafter on one GPU and resumes the judge for 2,000 more steps on the other seven, then evaluates four commit rules. Neither round 2b nor the drafter fine-tune has run yet; everything in this section is code that exists, not a result.

What the paper is, in each outcome

ifthen the contribution is
the judge clears the free rule's frontier per-slot acceptance of an external draft on a block-diffusion MoE, which no causal verifier can do — the intended result
the judge only matches a no-draft control certainty forcing replicated on an MoE block-diffusion model; publishable, but not the drafter claim
neither — today's position the mechanism analysis itself: the next-token residue at filled slots, the sycophancy of draft context, the blind-marginal ceiling, and a training-free rule that is free and accuracy-neutral. A weaker paper, but an honest and useful one.
